newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Thousands more reported heading to Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Thousands more reported heading to Rwanda.

text.p: Zairean rebel plans)
By Christian Jennings
Thousands more refugees, tracked by U.S. satellites, trekked through eastern Zaire towards Rwanda on Wednesday, further weakening the case for a U.N. intervention force.

The U.N.'s World Food Programme reported that as many as 100,000 Hutu refugees were on the road, the possible vanguard of a second mass exodus to the homeland they fled in panic after the Rwandan genocide and civil war in 1994.

"There are strong indications that a large movement of people from the Bukavu area are heading north towards Goma. We believe there could be more than 100,000," WFP spokeswoman Michele Quintaglie said in Nairobi.
Later, she said a U.N. assessment team had been allowed into Bukavu by Zairean rebels late on Wednesday, but had so far been unable to give more precise reports.
An estimated 700,000 Hutus are still thought to be in Zaire, after 500,000 others walked back into Rwanda from Goma between November 15 and 19.
A second mass movement would almost certainly lead the world to call off plans to send a Canadian-led humanitarian mission to the region.

Hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees have returned to Rwanda to escape fighting between Zairean rebels, supported by Rwanda, and soldiers from Rwanda's Hutu-dominated ex-army and militias, who organised the 1994 genocide of Rwanda's minority Tutsis.
The U.N. refugee agency in Goma said on Wednesday a large number of Rwandan refugees from the Bukavu area were moving north on the west of Lake Kivu towards Goma.
"There is a substantial number of refugees moving northwards at the moment," Filippo Grandi, head of the UNHCR in the town told Reuters.
"We are receiving information from local staff, local authorities and American intelligence satellites," he said, adding the estimate of those on the move varied enormously.

A planning meeting in Stuttgart on the intervention force will take place on Friday, according to the U.N.'s special envoy for the crisis, Raymond Chretien. But he suggested the force could be quite different from the 10,000-plus armed force originally envisaged.

"I'm told that today and tomorrow you can see a few tens of thousands more getting back into Rwanda, especially from the region of Bukavu in eastern Zaire," he told Canadian television. "The more refugees coming into Rwanda, of course the less need for a strong military intervention."

U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday the United States had made no final decision on involvement. Earlier, Defence Secretary William Perry said the U.S. was preparing a military air relief operation.
France, an enthusiastic advocate of armed intervention, said the humanitarian problem remained enormous and stepped up pressure on the U.S. to provide troops.
"It would be unbelievable to us that a great democracy like the United States would not be moved by a human tragedy of this magnitude," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said.

Aid officials argue the world focused on last weekend's mass exodus of some half-a-million Hutu refugees from eastern Zaire to Rwanda to the exclusion of an estimated 500,000 in the Bukavu area further south.
Journalists in the area said refugees emerging from the bush into which they had fled to avoid fighting said there were large numbers of people behind them.

A leader of the victorious rebel force that routed the Zairean army and pushed Hutu extremists from the refugee camps, triggering the refugee exodus to Rwanda, laid out plans on Wednesday to tax and administer the area it controls.
"We will start to tax the local people so that the schools work, markets are open and doctors can be paid," military leader Andre Kassesse told a rally in Goma, near the Rwandan border.
Zaire suspended outspoken army chief of staff General Eluki Monga on Wednesday for saying a multinational force was no longer needed in Zaire.
General Eluki had previously blamed the government for the army's pitiful showing against the rebels, saying it was starved of money to pay and equip troops.
